Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events

Negative Appraisals.value: There is something about me that made the event happen
I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me
Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation

issues.item: Triggers: Offender Cues: Seeing the offender
issues.explanation: For a combat trauma profile, 'seeing the offender' is hard to reconcile clinically because combat usually involves enemy forces or chaotic threat contexts rather than a single identifiable offender encountered later. This item fits interpersonal assault formulations better than combat.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Hypervigilance towards people: vigilant for dangerous people
issues.explanation: The profile's active formulation centers Triggers ↔ Maladaptive Strategies and Triggers → Negative Appraisals, with Threat inactive. Yet 'hypervigilance towards dangerous people' is primarily a current-threat item. In this profile there are no Threat items, and the other strategies are avoidance of social contact/relationships. This makes the hypervigilance item pull toward a threat-monitoring presentation not otherwise represented in the selected nodes.

vignette:
Amara was nineteen when her convoy was ambushed in southern Afghanistan, and she has never stopped believing that she caused it. She had been distracted that night-a letter from her mother about her younger brother's illness had arrived that morning, and she could not stop thinking about it. The patrol was supposed to be routine, moving through a village after dark. Helicopters had been passing overhead all evening, their rotors a familiar sound she barely registered until the ambush began. When the first shots came, she froze. A friend from her unit-Marcus, who had taught her how to tie a tourniquet-took the hit that might have been meant for her. She has replayed that moment so many times that it no longer feels like a memory: the dark alley, the rotor wash kicking up dust, the sight of Marcus falling. And the thought that followed, cold and certain: There is something about me that made this happen. Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation. Somebody else would have acted.

Two years later, at twenty-one, Amara works as a counselor at a community center for at-risk youth. She chose the job hoping it would help her feel useful again, but the work has only deepened her conviction that she is no longer capable of doing the things that used to define her. A client mentions their family in passing-a mother, a brother-and Amara feels the familiar tightness in her chest. She changes the subject quickly, then spends the rest of the session wondering if that reveals something broken in her. The sound of a helicopter from the nearby hospital pad makes her jump out of her chair; she excuses herself to the restroom and does not come back until the noise has faded. Her colleagues have started to notice, and she knows they are talking about her. She has stopped going to team lunches. She deleted her social media accounts. She cannot watch movies that show war, and she stopped answering calls from the few friends she had before deployment because she is certain they would see how diminished she is.

It is the darkness that hits her hardest. When daylight saving ends and the evenings get longer, she comes home from work and sits in her apartment with every light on. The moment she switches off the lamp, she sees the alley again. The thought arrives on its own: I am no longer capable of protecting anyone. I could not protect myself or Marcus. That belief sends her back into herself-she cancels plans, declines invitations to start new friendships or relationships, tells herself that the person she was died in that alley and the person she is now does not deserve connection. The longer she avoids people, the more convinced she becomes that she was always flawed, that the ambush merely exposed what was already there. It is a loop that tightens over weeks, feeding itself.

The avoidance does not reduce the triggers; it sharpens them. Because she refuses to watch any media about combat, she has no way to habituate to helicopter sounds, and every unexpected rotor overhead sends her heart racing. Because she avoids talking to anyone from her old unit, a single well-intentioned question about her family can derail an entire day. And the more she isolates, the more she believes she is unworthy of the community she has pulled away from. She has not dated since returning home; the thought of someone discovering what she did-or did not do-makes her feel physically ill.

What finally brought Amara to seek help was a Tuesday afternoon in the counseling center. A young client, a boy whose mother had recently been deployed, started talking about how much he missed her. Amara felt the floor tilt. She excused herself, locked herself in the supply closet in the dark-it was the only place she could go-and sat there shaking for twenty minutes, her flashlight doing nothing to push away the image of Marcus. Afterward, her supervisor found her and asked if she was okay. Amara said she was fine, but she knew she was not. She had come to believe that the only way out was to stop running, but she was terrified that facing the memories would confirm everything she already suspected: that she was the one at fault, that she could not be fixed, and that someone else would have walked away from that alley whole.
